explanations.explanation: Egypt it is, friend. The LORD says, "When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son." (Hosea 11:1) Notice that the love and the calling sit side by side in this one verse. That's a good thing to hold onto before the rest of this chapter gets rough.

Babylon is a big name in the Bible, so I get why it jumped out. But here the LORD says, "…out of Egypt I called My son." (Hosea 11:1) Babylon never comes up in these verses. Egypt is the place He called His son out of.
Moab might have crossed your mind, and that's fair. But the LORD says, "…out of Egypt I called My son." (Hosea 11:1) Moab isn't in this passage at all. Egypt is the place He called His son out of.

I get the hope, friend, but it's the other way around. The text says, "But the more I called Israel, the farther they departed from Me." (Hosea 11:2) So the calling went up and the distance went up with it. That is a LOT of walking in the wrong direction.

False, and the text is blunt about it. "But the more I called Israel, the farther they departed from Me." (Hosea 11:2) The more He called, the farther they went. I think that must have been a hard thing for a loving Father to watch.

The Baals, that's right. Hosea 11:2 says, "They sacrificed to the Baals and burned incense to carved images." Baals were false gods, and the text puts them right next to carved images. Israel was walking away from the LORD while sacrificing to the Baals.

Molech does show up elsewhere in Scripture (Leviticus 18:21), so I see why it came to mind. But this verse names a different one: "They sacrificed to the Baals and burned incense to carved images." (Hosea 11:2) Molech isn't mentioned here. The Baals are the answer.

Dagon was a god of the Philistines (Judges 16:23), so I see why it came to mind. But Hosea 11:2 says, "They sacrificed to the Baals and burned incense to carved images." Dagon never shows up in these verses. It's the Baals this time.

Wish that were so, friend, but the text says otherwise. The LORD says, "It was I who taught Ephraim to walk, taking them by the arms, but they never realized that it was I who healed them." (Hosea 11:3) The word is never. They got the healing and missed who gave it.

False, and that stings a little. "…they never realized that it was I who healed them." (Hosea 11:3) The LORD took Ephraim by the arms and taught them to walk, and they never realized it was He who healed them. I think that's the kind of thing a dad remembers.
Cords of kindness, you got it. The LORD says, "I led them with cords of kindness, with ropes of love…" (Hosea 11:4) Ropes, and every one of them made of love. That's about as gentle as leading gets.

A rod of iron sounds tough, but that's not what the LORD says here. He says, "I led them with cords of kindness, with ropes of love…" (Hosea 11:4) He led with kindness. No iron anywhere in this verse.

The yoke is in the verse, but it goes the opposite way. The LORD says, "I lifted the yoke from their necks…" (Hosea 11:4) He took the weight off. And He led them "…with cords of kindness, with ropes of love…"

Feed, friend. The LORD says, "I lifted the yoke from their necks and bent down to feed them." (Hosea 11:4) Think about that picture. He didn't just take the weight off, He bent down to meet them where they were.
I can see why scold crossed your mind after verse 2. But verse 4 says, "I lifted the yoke from their necks and bent down to feed them." Nobody gets scolded in this verse. He bent down and fed them.

Count isn't in this verse, friend. Hosea 11:4 says, "I lifted the yoke from their necks and bent down to feed them." The yoke comes off and He bends down to feed them. Nothing in it is about counting. It's all care.

That's the reason the text gives, baker. "Will they not return to the land of Egypt and be ruled by Assyria because they refused to repent?" (Hosea 11:5) Assyria is the one named to rule them. The reason is the refusing, nothing else.

An army problem makes sense on a map, but the text gives a different reason. It says Israel would be ruled by Assyria "…because they refused to repent?" (Hosea 11:5) Army size never comes up in these verses.

Kings do get blamed a lot, but the text doesn't say that here. It says, "…because they refused to repent?" (Hosea 11:5) No king is mentioned in this verse. The reason it gives is about the people refusing to repent.

True, and it's a sober one. "Though they call to the Most High, He will by no means exalt them." (Hosea 11:7) The Most High is another name for God. I think this is a heavy verse, so let's just let it be heavy for a second. And remember, friend, the story isn't over.

I understand wanting that one to be false. But the text says, "Though they call to the Most High, He will by no means exalt them." (Hosea 11:7) That's a hard line to read. The good news is the message isn't finished yet, and there's more coming.

explanations.answer: How could I give you up
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend! After all of that, the LORD asks, "How could I give you up, O Ephraim?" (Hosea 11:8) Then the next line asks, "How could I surrender you, O Israel?" Right after the hard warnings comes a question full of love.

That's what you might expect after all those warnings. But the LORD says, "How could I give you up, O Ephraim?" (Hosea 11:8) He doesn't ask why He should keep Ephraim. He asks how He could give Ephraim up.

After a sword flashing through cities, that sounds like it could be next. But it's not what He says. The LORD asks, "How could I give you up, O Ephraim? How could I surrender you, O Israel?" (Hosea 11:8)
Compassion, you got it. The LORD says, "My heart is turned within Me; My compassion is stirred!" (Hosea 11:8) That's God speaking about His own heart. The warnings were real, and so is this.

Jealousy shows up in other places in Scripture, like Exodus 34:14, but not in this verse. Here the LORD says, "My heart is turned within Me; My compassion is stirred!" (Hosea 11:8) Compassion is what's stirring in Him.
Pride doesn't make an appearance here, friend. The LORD says, "My heart is turned within Me; My compassion is stirred!" (Hosea 11:8) What stirs in Him is compassion.

After verse 6 I get why you'd think so, but this verse turns it around. The LORD says, "I will not execute the full fury of My anger…" (Hosea 11:9) So the answer is no. The text really does say He will not.

False, and I'm glad it is. The LORD says, "I will not execute the full fury of My anger; I will not destroy Ephraim again." (Hosea 11:9) The text says it plainly, and it comes right after the warnings.

explanations.answer: He is God and not man
explanations.explanation: That's exactly the reason He gives. "For I am God and not man—the Holy One among you—and I will not come in wrath." (Hosea 11:9) The reason is who He is. Nothing Ephraim did gets listed as the cause.

That would be a tidy ending, but the text doesn't say it. The LORD gives this reason: "For I am God and not man…" (Hosea 11:9) Ephraim's repenting isn't mentioned in these verses. His reason is about who He is.

explanations.answer: The prophet begged Him to stop
explanations.explanation: It's a natural guess, since the prophet Amos pleads for Jacob in Amos 7:2. But in this passage nobody begs Him. The LORD says, "For I am God and not man—the Holy One among you—and I will not come in wrath." (Hosea 11:9) That's His own reason, in His own words.

I can see why you'd say true, since verse 6 was rough. But verse 9 ends differently. The LORD says, "…I am God and not man—the Holy One among you—and I will not come in wrath." (Hosea 11:9) The text says He will not.

False, friend. The LORD says, "…I am God and not man—the Holy One among you—and I will not come in wrath." (Hosea 11:9) He calls Himself the Holy One among them. And the words right after are "I will not…"
A lion, yes! "They will walk after the LORD; He will roar like a lion." (Hosea 11:10) The text puts the roar and the walking together. And the whole thing is about what comes next.
A bear can sure growl, I'll give you that. But the verse names a different animal. It says, "He will roar like a lion." (Hosea 11:10) The bear isn't in this verse.
A wolf howls more than it roars, friend. Hosea 11:10 says, "He will roar like a lion." A lion is the one that fits this verse.

A roar from a lion would make most of us run, so I get the guess. But the text goes the other way. "When He roars, His children will come trembling from the west." (Hosea 11:10) They come toward Him, not away.

False, friend. "When He roars, His children will come trembling from the west." (Hosea 11:10) They come trembling, and the text never says they run away. I think those must be some shaky steps. But they are steps in the right direction.

In their homes, friend. The LORD says, "Then I will settle them in their homes, declares the LORD." (Hosea 11:11) Settled, and in their own homes. The one who calls them is the one who puts them there.

Egypt appears in the verse, but only as a place they come from. The text says they come "…like birds from Egypt…" and then the LORD says, "…I will settle them in their homes…" (Hosea 11:11) Their homes are where they end up.

explanations.answer: In a city by the sea
explanations.explanation: A seaside city sounds nice, but the text doesn't say that. The LORD says, "Then I will settle them in their homes, declares the LORD." (Hosea 11:11) No coast mentioned. It's their homes.
